problem: Source: 'whenever I spoke, they sounded in my voice to his ear, and their echo toned every answer he gave me.' Modern invents 'They colored my every word and action' and drops that it is his hearing and his answers that are affected.
final_text: Not that St. John harbored any spirit of unchristian revenge—not that he would have harmed a hair on my head if he could. By both nature and principle, he was above petty vengeance. He had forgiven me for saying I scorned him and his love. But he had not forgotten the words. As long as he and I both lived, he never would forget them. I saw by his look, whenever he turned to me, that they hung permanently in the air between us. Whenever I spoke, he heard them in my voice, and their echo colored every answer he gave me.

problem: Source ends 'he was in reality become no longer flesh, but marble; his eye was a cold, bright, blue gem; his tongue a speaking instrument—nothing more.' Modern invents 'a marble guardian angel... still protecting me, still watching over me' (reversing the point) and drops the gem/instrument images; 'the corrupt man within him' softened and 'austere charm' lost.
final_text: He didn't stop talking to me. He even called me each morning to join him at his desk as usual. But I fear the corrupt man inside him took a pleasure the pure Christian did not share—pleasure in showing how skillfully he could, while acting and speaking exactly as always, drain from every deed and every phrase the interest and approval that had once given his language and manner a certain austere charm. To me, he had in reality become no longer flesh, but marble. His eye was a cold, bright, blue gem; his tongue, a speaking instrument—nothing more.

problem: After 'No ruth met my ruth' the modern invents 'He hadn't given himself to me... different species... quietly confident that he was right' and drops the source's estrangement/no yearning for reconciliation, the tears blistering the page with no effect on his 'stone or metal' heart, and his pointed kindness to his sisters 'not by malice, but on principle'. Also 'indignation' became 'frustration' and 'soon kill' became 'slowly kill'.
final_text: All this was torture—refined, lingering torture. It kept up a slow fire of indignation and a trembling grief that harassed and crushed me completely. I felt how—if I were his wife—this good man, pure as a deep, sunless spring, could soon kill me without drawing a single drop of blood from my veins, and without staining his crystal conscience with even the faintest mark of crime. I felt this especially when I tried to win him over. No pity met my pity. He felt no suffering from our estrangement—no longing for reconciliation. More than once my fast-falling tears blistered the page we were both bent over, but they had no more effect on him than if his heart had truly been made of stone or metal. Meanwhile, he was somewhat kinder than usual to his sisters. As if afraid that mere coldness would not fully convince me how completely I was banished and banned, he added the force of contrast. And this, I am sure, he did not out of malice, but on principle.

problem: Dropped 'which he had been contemplating as I approached' — he was already absorbed in the moon.
final_text: "I hope we are friends," came the unmoved reply. He continued watching the rising moon, which he had been gazing at as I approached.

problem: 'the suggestions of pride and ire' reduced to 'pride'; anger dropped (and 'those feelings' then refers to both).
final_text: This, spoken in a cool, even tone, was both humiliating and baffling. If I'd listened to my pride and anger, I would have walked away at once. But something worked in me more powerfully than those feelings. I deeply respected my cousin's talent and principles. His friendship meant a great deal to me. Losing it was hard to bear. I wouldn't give up the attempt to regain it so easily.

problem: 'between Nature and Grace' (theological: nature vs divine grace) rendered 'nature and duty', changing the religious meaning.
final_text: A very long silence followed. What struggle between nature and grace took place in him during that pause, I cannot say. Only strange gleams flickered in his eyes, and dark shadows crossed his face. At last he spoke.

problem: Hedge 'I begin to think' dropped: 'would, I begin to think, be almost equivalent to committing suicide' made a flat assertion.
final_text: "I am. God did not give me my life to throw away. To do as you wish would, I'm beginning to think, be nearly the same as suicide. And besides, before I make any final decision about leaving England, I need to know for certain whether I can't do more good by staying than by going."

problem: Source ends with a question, 'You think of Mr. Rochester?', which Jane answers 'by silence' in 35.42; modern makes it a statement.
final_text: "I know where your heart turns and what it clings to. The attachment you cherish is sinful and unsanctioned. You should have destroyed it long ago. Now you should be ashamed even to mention it. You're thinking of Mr. Rochester?"

problem: Source ends 'and now believed he had forgiven me once more.' Modern invents 'But I saw he had not... The forgiveness was a performance. Beneath it, the steel remained.' Also 'the sequel showed' narrowed to 'the rest of the evening' and 'once more' dropped.
final_text: But I was forced to face him again at supper. During the meal he appeared just as composed as usual. I had thought he would barely speak to me, and I was certain he had abandoned his marriage plan. What followed proved me wrong on both counts. He addressed me exactly in his usual manner—or what had lately become his usual manner—carefully polite. No doubt he had called on the Holy Spirit to subdue the anger I'd provoked, and now believed he had forgiven me once more.

problem: Modern invents Revelation 22 content ('the river of the water of life, and the tree with its twelve kinds of fruit') and pulls in 35.79's 'city with no need of sun or moon'; drops the source's uncurtained window/candle, 'bending over the great old Bible', God dwelling with men, wiping away all tears, 'no more death, neither sorrow nor crying'.
final_text: For the evening reading before prayers, he chose the twenty-first chapter of Revelation. It was always a pleasure to listen as the words of the Bible fell from his lips. Never did his fine voice sound so sweet and full—never was his manner so impressive in its noble simplicity—as when he delivered the words of God. And tonight that voice took a more solemn tone, and his manner a more thrilling meaning, as he sat in the midst of his household circle (the May moon shining in through the uncurtained window, making the candle on the table almost unnecessary)—as he sat there, bending over the great old Bible, and described from its page the vision of the new heaven and the new earth. He told how God would come to dwell with men, how He would wipe away all tears from their eyes, and promised that there should be no more death, neither sorrow nor crying, nor any more pain, because the former things had passed away.

problem: Dropped 'whom the temptations of the world and the flesh were luring' and flattened 'He asked, he urged, he claimed the boon of a brand snatched from the burning' to 'He pleaded for'; 'eleventh hour' allusion lost.
final_text: In the prayer that followed, all his energy gathered and all his stern passion awoke. He was in deep earnest, wrestling with God, determined to prevail. He begged for strength for the fainthearted. He asked for guidance for wanderers from the fold—for a return, even at the eleventh hour, for those whom the temptations of the world and the flesh were luring from the narrow path. He asked, he urged, he claimed the gift of a brand snatched from the burning. Earnestness is always deeply solemn. First, as I listened to that prayer, I wondered at his; then, as it continued and rose, I was touched by it, and at last awed. He felt the greatness and goodness of his purpose so sincerely that others who heard him plead for it could not but feel it too.

problem: 'I cannot give you up to perdition as a vessel of wrath' reduced to 'I cannot abandon you to ruin' — the biblical 'vessel of wrath' and the sense of damnation are lost.
final_text: "Thank you, Jane. As I said, I'll return from Cambridge in two weeks. That time is yours for reflection. If I listened to human pride, I would say nothing more about marriage. But I listen to my duty, and I keep my first aim firmly in view—to do all things for the glory of God. My Master was patient, and so will I be. I cannot give you up to damnation as a vessel of wrath. Repent—decide, while there's still time. Remember, we're told to work while it is day—warned that the night comes when no one can work. Remember the fate of Dives, who had his good things in this life. God give you strength to choose the better part which shall not be taken from you!"

problem: 'I contended with my inward dimness of vision, before which clouds yet rolled' rendered 'behind which something still churned' — invented image.
final_text: "My prayers are heard!" St. John exclaimed. He pressed his hand more firmly on my head, as if claiming me. He put his arm around me—almost as if he loved me. I say almost—I knew the difference. I had felt what it was to be loved. But, like him, I had now pushed love aside and thought only of duty. I struggled against my inward dimness of vision, before which clouds still rolled. Sincerely, deeply, urgently, I longed to do what was right—and only that. "Show me, show me the path!" I begged of Heaven. I was more excited than I had ever been—and whatever followed, the reader may judge for themselves whether it was the effect of that excitement.

problem: Dropped 'that thrilled it through, and passed at once to my head and extremities' — the feeling spreading through her body.
final_text: The house was completely still. I believe everyone except St. John and me had gone to bed. The single candle was dying out. The room was full of moonlight. My heart beat fast and hard—I could hear its throb. Suddenly it stood still, seized by a feeling beyond description that thrilled right through it and passed at once to my head and limbs. The feeling was not like an electric shock, but it was just as sharp, strange, and startling. It acted on my senses as if they had been asleep until now, and were suddenly jolted wide awake. They rose, expectant—eye and ear waiting. The flesh trembled on my bones.

problem: Source ends 'my soul rushed out in gratitude at His feet. I rose from the thanksgiving—took a resolve—and lay down, unscared, enlightened—eager but for the daylight.' Modern invents 'reach beyond the visible world, as it were', 'Not through words. Through something deeper.', 'I knew what I had to do', and drops 'at His feet' and lying down 'unscared, enlightened—eager but for the daylight' (which sets up 36.0 'The daylight came').
final_text: I broke away from St. John, who had followed and would have held me back. It was my turn to take command. My powers were awake and active. I told him not to question or comment. I told him to leave me alone. I must and would be alone. He obeyed at once. Where there is energy to command well enough, obedience never fails. I went up to my room, locked myself in, fell on my knees, and prayed in my own way—a different way from St. John's, but effective in its own fashion. I seemed to come very near a mighty Spirit, and my soul rushed out in gratitude at His feet. I rose from the thanksgiving—made my resolution—and lay down, unafraid, enlightened—eager only for the daylight.

problem: Source's closing image — the shock of feeling 'like the earthquake which shook the foundations of Paul and Silas's prison', opening the soul's cell, the cry vibrating thrice, the spirit exulting 'independent of the cumbrous body' — is dropped and replaced by invented 'The extraordinary effect on me confirmed this. I felt as though I had been called—not by mortal voice, but by something higher.'
final_text: It was still two hours until breakfast. I filled the time walking softly around my room, pondering the experience that had given my plans their new direction. I recalled the sensation I had felt—for I could recall it, with all its indescribable strangeness. I recalled the voice I had heard. Again I asked where it had come from, as uselessly as before. It had seemed to be inside me—not in the external world. I asked myself whether it was just a nervous impression—a delusion. I couldn't conceive or believe it. It was more like an inspiration. The wondrous shock of feeling had come like the earthquake that shook the foundations of Paul and Silas's prison. It had opened the doors of the soul's cell and loosed its chains. It had woken the soul from its sleep, and it sprang up trembling, listening, aghast. Then a cry vibrated three times on my startled ear, and in my quaking heart, and through my spirit—which neither feared nor shook, but exulted as if in joy at the success of one effort it had been privileged to make, independent of the cumbersome body.

problem: Source ends 'Once more on the road to Thornfield, I felt like the messenger-pigeon flying home.' Modern replaces this with invented 'Once I had been penniless. Now I had means. The coach carried me away.' Also 'one summer evening' dropped and 'my whole fortune' reduced to 'my last coins'.
final_text: I left Moor House at three in the afternoon. Soon after four I stood at the Whitcross signpost, waiting for the coach that would take me to distant Thornfield. In the silence of those lonely roads and empty hills, I heard it approaching from far away. It was the same coach from which, a year ago, I had stepped down on this very spot one summer evening—so desolate, hopeless, and purposeless! It stopped at my signal. I climbed in—this time not forced to hand over my whole fortune as the price of my seat. Once more on the road to Thornfield, I felt like a homing pigeon flying home.

problem: Modern appends '"How far is Thornfield Hall from here?" I asked eagerly.' — this is 36.14's line, now duplicated. Also 'North-Midland' dropped from 'the stern North-Midland moors of Morton'.
final_text: It was a journey of thirty-six hours. I had set out from Whitcross on a Tuesday afternoon. Early Thursday morning the coach stopped to water the horses at a roadside inn, set amid scenery whose green hedges, broad fields, and gentle hills—how mild compared to the stern North-Midland moors of Morton!—greeted my eyes like the features of a once-familiar face. Yes, I recognized this landscape. I was sure we were near my destination.

problem: 'under the ray of her star' (Hope's star) became invented 'beneath the morning sky'; 'distracted with a revengeful fury tracking and scourging me' became 'driven half-mad with anguish'; 'How I ran sometimes!', the woods, the welcomed single trees and glimpses of meadow and hill are replaced by a generic 'How eagerly I strained my eyes toward the familiar landscape!'.
final_text: The suggestion was sensible, yet I couldn't force myself to act on it. I so dreaded an answer that would crush me with despair. To prolong doubt was to prolong hope. I might yet see the Hall once more under the light of hope's star. There was the stile before me—the very fields I had hurried through, blind, deaf, distracted, with a vengeful fury hunting and lashing me, on the morning I fled from Thornfield. Before I fully knew what I'd decided, I was in the midst of them. How fast I walked! How I ran sometimes! How I looked ahead to catch the first view of the well-known woods! With what feelings I welcomed single trees I knew, and familiar glimpses of meadow and hill between them!

problem: After 'or on the pavement in front' the modern invents 'If so, I could meet him this very minute. Is there not a chance? A possibility?' and drops the source's 'Could I but see him!—but a moment! Surely... I should not be so mad as to run to him?... God bless him! What then? Who would be hurt...? I rave: perhaps at this moment he is watching the sun rise over the Pyrenees, or on the tideless sea of the south.'
final_text: At last the woods rose up. The rookery clustered dark. A loud cawing broke the morning stillness. Strange joy filled me. On I hurried. Another field crossed—a lane threaded—and there were the courtyard walls and the back buildings. The house itself, the rookery still hid. "My first glimpse shall be from the front," I decided, "where the bold battlements will strike my eye at once, and where I can pick out my master's very window. Perhaps he'll be standing at it—he rises early. Perhaps he's walking in the orchard, or on the paved walk in front. If only I could see him!—just for a moment! Surely, in that case, I wouldn't be so mad as to run to him? I can't tell—I'm not certain. And if I did—what then? God bless him! What then? Who would be hurt by my once more tasting the life his glance can give me? I'm raving: perhaps at this moment he is watching the sun rise over the Pyrenees, or over the tideless sea of the south."

problem: Dropped the crows' imagined questions ('What affectation of diffidence was this at first?... what stupid regardlessness now?') and 'very bold and reckless' reduced to 'bolder'.
final_text: The crows sailing overhead may have watched me taking this survey. I wonder what they thought. They must have noticed I was very cautious and timid at first, and that gradually I grew very bold and reckless. A peek, then a long stare. Then a departure from my hiding place and a drift into the meadow. Then a sudden stop, full in front of the grand house, and a long, hard look straight at it. "Why that show of shyness at first?" they might have asked. "Why this stupid carelessness now?"

problem: Modern invents 'Not just a veil was lifted—a mask was removed... a skeleton. A death's head, cold and grinning' and drops the source's climax: he clasps her in both arms, calls her name, drops his burden, no longer fears waking her — 'He thought his love slept sweetly: he finds she is stone dead.' This is the parable that sets up 36.24.
final_text: A lover finds his beloved asleep on a mossy bank. He wants to catch a glimpse of her fair face without waking her. He creeps softly over the grass, careful to make no sound. He pauses—thinking she's stirred. He retreats. Not for anything would he be seen. All is still. He advances again. He bends over her. A light veil rests on her features. He lifts it, bends lower. His eyes anticipate the vision of beauty—warm, blooming, lovely in sleep. How hurried was their first glance! But how they fix! How he starts! How he suddenly and fiercely clasps in both arms the body he didn't dare, a moment ago, touch with his finger! How he calls a name aloud, and drops his burden, and gazes at it wildly! He grasps and cries and gazes like this because he no longer fears waking her with any sound he can make—any movement. He thought his love slept sweetly. He finds she is stone dead.

problem: Source ends 'Dreadful question: there was no one here to answer it—not even dumb sign, mute token.' Modern invents 'one I dreaded having answered, yet felt compelled to ask' and drops that there was no one and nothing to answer.
final_text: And there was the silence of death around it—the solitude of a desolate wasteland. No wonder that letters sent here had never been answered. You might as well have mailed them to a tomb. The black grimness of the stones told how the Hall had fallen—by fire. But how was it started? What story lay behind this disaster? What losses beyond wood and stone and plaster had followed? Had lives been ruined as well as property? If so, whose? Terrible question—and there was no one here to answer it, not even a silent sign or mute token.

problem: Source ends 'My eye involuntarily wandered to the grey church tower near the gates, and I asked, "Is he with Damer de Rochester, sharing the shelter of his narrow marble house?"' Modern invents eyes wandering over the ruins then 'toward the sky above the ruins, as if searching for something more', losing the fear that he is dead and buried. Also hedge 'I thought' dropped.
final_text: Wandering around the shattered walls and through the devastated interior, I gathered evidence that the catastrophe was not recent. Winter snows, I thought, had drifted through that empty arch. Winter rains had beaten in through hollow windows. Among the soaked piles of rubble, spring had encouraged new growth—grass and weeds sprouted between the stones and fallen beams. And oh! where, in the meantime, was the unfortunate owner of this wreck? In what country? Under what circumstances? My eyes wandered involuntarily to the grey church tower near the gates, and I asked, "Is he with Damer de Rochester, sharing the shelter of his narrow marble house?"

problem: 'this governess not twenty' rendered 'barely twenty' — changes her age from under twenty to about twenty.
final_text: "I'm coming to that, ma'am. Mr. Edward fell in love with her. The servants said they'd never seen anyone so smitten. He followed her everywhere. They used to watch him—servants do, you know, ma'am—and he was devoted to her beyond everything. Though nobody but him thought her all that beautiful. She was a little, small thing, they said—almost like a child. I never saw her myself, but I heard Leah the housemaid talk about her. Leah liked her well enough. Mr. Rochester was about forty, and she wasn't yet twenty. You see, when gentlemen his age fall in love with girls, they're often like men bewitched. Well, he would marry her."

problem: The innkeeper's mild 'Bless you, no!' became the oath 'God, no!' — a register change for this respectable ex-butler.
final_text: "Leave England? Bless you, no! He wouldn't so much as cross the doorstep—except at night, when he'd walk like a ghost around the grounds and through the orchard. As if he'd lost his mind—which, in my opinion, he had. Because before that slip of a governess crossed his path, you'd never have met a more spirited, bolder, keener gentleman. He wasn't a man given to drinking, gambling, or horse racing, as some are, and he wasn't especially handsome. But he had courage and a will of his own, if ever a man did. I knew him from a boy, you see—and for my part, I've often wished Miss Eyre had been sunk in the sea before she ever came to Thornfield Hall."

problem: Source: 'I witnessed, and several more witnessed, Mr. Rochester ascend through the sky-light on to the roof; we heard him call "Bertha!" We saw him approach her; and then, ma'am, she yelled and gave a spring'. Modern reverses the order (call before climb), drops the name 'Bertha!' and the several witnesses, and invents 'We shouted for him to come down—it was too dangerous.' Also 'his mad wife out of her cell' softened to 'his wife out of her room'. (Ending on the leap is kept because source 36.53 repeats 'The next minute she lay smashed on the pavement'.)
final_text: "Yes, indeed he was. And he went up to the attics when everything was burning above and below. He got the servants out of their beds and helped them down himself, and went back to get his mad wife out of her cell. And then they called out to him that she was on the roof. She was standing there, waving her arms above the battlements, shouting so loud they could hear her a mile away. I saw her and heard her with my own eyes. She was a big woman, with long black hair. We could see it streaming against the flames as she stood there. I saw—and several others saw—Mr. Rochester climb through the skylight onto the roof. We heard him call 'Bertha!' We saw him approach her. And then, ma'am, she yelled and gave a leap—"

problem: 'The other eye inflamed: he lost the sight of that also' rendered 'He lost the other eye too' — implies the eye itself was lost and drops the inflammation; the distinction matters for his later partial recovery of sight in that eye.
final_text: "It was his own courage, and you might say his kindness, in a way, ma'am. He wouldn't leave the house till everyone else was out. As he came down the great staircase at last, after Mrs. Rochester threw herself from the battlements, there was a massive crash—everything collapsed. He was pulled from the ruins alive, but badly injured. A beam had partly protected him, but one eye was destroyed, and one hand was so crushed that the surgeon, Mr. Carter, had to amputate it immediately. The other eye became inflamed, and he lost the sight of that one too. He's now helpless—blind and crippled."
